title: Infra runbook: GPU fleet capacity, cloud accounts & networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD
author: Samira Khan
content:
Overview

This consolidated runbook documents operational procedures and engineering standards for: GPU fleet capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking controls, Terraform/IaC modules used by the GPU fleet, CI/CD and build pipelines for infra modules, and day-2 runbook steps for on-call and incident response. The target audience is infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners.

Goals
- Provide a single-source-of-truth for scaling and recovery actions that are safe for production.
- Reduce mean time to recovery (MTTR) for GPU-related incidents.
- Standardize Terraform module usage and CI/CD patterns to minimize drift.
- Document ownership, SLOs, and escalation paths.

Key definitions
- GPU pool: a logical group of instances (reserved/dedicated) running inference workloads.
- Capacity unit: 1 A100-80GB-equivalent GPU in our internal capacity model.
- Hot zone: region with >80% GPU utilization over a 5-minute rolling window.

Ownership and contacts
- Fleet owner: infra-gpu@redwood.com (Primary: Ethan Morales)
- Network owner: infra-networking@redwood.com (Primary: Lin Zhao)
- Terraform modules owner: infra-iac@redwood.com (Samira Khan)
- On-call rota: see /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks/oncall-rotation (pager duty)

SLOs and thresholds (fleet-level)
| Metric | Target | Alert threshold | Priority | Owner |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| GPU availability | 99.9% monthly | < 99.5% | P1 | infra-gpu |
| Pod scheduling latency | < 2s p50 | > 5s p95 | P2 | infra-platform |
| Autoscaler success rate | 99% | < 95% | P2 | infra-gpu |

Monitoring and alerts
- Dashboards: infra/gpu/fleet-overview, infra/gpu/region-usage, infra/network/vpc-health.
- Primary alerts (PagerDuty P1/P2):
  - GPU pool down (all nodes NotReady) -> P1
  - Hot zone sustained >90% for 10m -> P1 (capacity scaling recommended)
  - Autoscaler failing to provision new nodes -> P1
  - Terraform apply drift detected on core modules -> P2

Runbook: responding to a Hot Zone (sustained high utilization)
1) Triage (0-5 minutes)
   - Acknowledge alert in PagerDuty.
   - Open Slack #infra-gpu and post summary: region, pools affected, current utilization, recent deploys.
   - Check dashboards: GPU util, node counts, pod queue length.
2) Immediate mitigation (5-15 minutes)
   - If autoscaler healthy: increase autoscaler target temporarily (example: increase max_nodes from 200 -> 260).
     - CLI: gcloud compute instance-groups managed resize <ig-name> --size=260 --zone=<zone>
   - If autoscaler failing: manually launch capacity-per-policy (see manual scale table below).
   - If policy prohibits scaling (cost controls): trigger overflow routing to lower-cost model variant (see routing playbook).
3) Stabilize (15-60 minutes)
   - Verify new nodes registered, pods scheduled, and queue length dropping.
   - Monitor for regressions in latency and error rates.
4) Post-incident (after recovery)
   - Run a Terraform plan/apply to reconcile any manual changes (tagged: "post-hotzone-reconcile").
   - Create a postmortem if P1 or >1 hour user impact.

Manual scaling policy (table)
| Situation | Action | Minimum approvals | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Autoscaler responding slowly | Manual scale +20% | oncall + team lead | Use approved instance types only (see Allowed Instances below) |
| Autoscaler failing to create instances | Launch prebaked instances via cloud account runbook | oncall + infra-gpu lead | Follow cloud account networking steps to ensure correct service account |
| Cost-sensitive window | Route traffic to Dedicated lower-cost pools | infra-gpu lead | Requires change in routing policy; may increase latency |

Allowed Instances and sizing
| Instance type | GPU equivalent | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| a2-megagpu-16g | 1 | High memory workloads; preferred for large models |
| a2-highgpu-1g | 1/8 | Burst workloads allowed |
| nvidia-a100-80gb | 1 | Baseline capacity unit |

Terraform/IaC modules: usage and standards
- Module layout (canonical): modules/gpu_pool, modules/networking, modules/cloud_account, modules/iam, modules/monitoring.
- Published module versioning: Semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). Example module source in root repo: git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infra-modules.git//modules/gpu_pool?ref=v1.3.0
- Required checks before apply:
  1. terratest suite: make test-terraform-modules (unit/integration mocks).
  2. tfsec security scan: make tfsec-scan
  3. Plan approval via GitHub PROTECTED BRANCH requiring 2 approvers.

Example module usage (snippet):
```
module "gpu_pool_us_east" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infra-modules.git//modules/gpu_pool?ref=v1.3.0"
  name   = "gpu-pool-us-east"
  region = "us-east1"
  instance_type = "nvidia-a100-80gb"
  min_size = 10
  max_size = 200
  labels = { env = "prod", team = "inference" }
}
```

Terraform CI/CD and build pipeline (recommended pattern)
- Repo structure: infra-modules/ (modules), infra-live/ (env specific stacks).
- CI pipeline (GitHub Actions):
  - On PR: terraform fmt, terraform validate, terratest (fast subset), tfsec, tf-lint.
  - On merge to main: create plan artifact and require manual "apply" via workflow_dispatch in environments/prod with 2 reviewers.
- Governance: environment secrets (cloud keys) encrypted and accessible only via environment-level policies.

CI example workflow steps:
1) Checkout + setup terraform
2) run: terraform init -backend-config=...
3) run: terraform fmt -check
4) run: terraform validate
5) run: make test-terraform-modules (terratest)
6) run: tfsec
7) create plan artifact -> attach to release notes -> require approval

Network controls and cloud accounts
- Each cloud account must have: centralized VPC templates, standardized subnet sizing, egress NAT gateways, service-account mappings, and shared VPC peering where required.
- IAM: least-privilege service accounts for node bootstrapping and autoscaler; short-lived workload identity tokens for cluster autoscaling.
- Connectors: use central logging/monitoring peering with retention of 90 days for infra metrics.

Quick checks and commands
- Check GPU pool utilization: kubectl -n infra-gpu get hpa, kubectl top nodes --gpu | sort -r -k2 -n
- Check autoscaler logs: gcloud logging read "resource.type=gce_instance AND logName=projects/redwood/logs/autoscaler" --limit=50
- Terraform plan locally: TF_VAR_region=us-east1 make tf-plan TARGET=modules/gpu_pool

Drift detection and reconciliation
- Weekly: run scheduled Terraform plan for prod stacks and surface diffs into an internal ticket queue.
- When drift found: label tickets with "drift-urgent" if resource change impacts availability.
- For low-risk drift: schedule a normal change with review.

Safe rollouts and module upgrades
1) Publish module changes on feature branch.
2) Run full module test matrix (terratest across small real infra or emulation).
3) Bump module version, create PR in infra-live with plan.
4) Canary apply in staging -> smoke tests -> apply in prod with 2 approvers.

On-call play: autoscaler failure (P1)
1) Acknowledge and collect logs (last 1 hour).
2) Check cloud quotas and GCP/Azure API health pages.
3) If quota exhausted: request quota increase via cloud console (document the submitted ticket number) and manually provision fallback nodes.
4) If nodes stuck in provisioning: redeploy instance template (append timestamp tag) and re-run instance group recreate.

Post-incident checklist
- Document timeline and root cause.
- Tag all Terraform/CI runs involved.
- Run an emergency capacity stress test in staging to validate fixes.
- Schedule a retrospective and follow-up tasks with owners and due dates.

Appendix: common troubleshooting commands
- kubectl get nodes -o wide
- kubectl describe pod <pod> -n inference
- gcloud compute instances list --filter="labels:gpu_pool"
- terraform state list | grep gpu
